title: Value of U.S. mineral production rose last year (Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 release)
key_claim: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 reports the United States remained reliant on imports from China as a major source for 14 of the 33 critical minerals for which it most depends on imports, and that China restricts the export of 14 minerals (antimony to tungsten) to the United States; net imports of processed metals and materials more than doubled by value from $77 billion in 2024 to $185 billion in 2025; the release coincides with the President's 'Project Vault' critical-minerals stockpile and a January proclamation on imports of processed critical minerals.
frame_summary: The USGS documents deepening US dependence on imported and Chinese-controlled critical minerals, framing minerals as central to national security and economic stability.
notes: Tier 1 US government primary data. Anchors the physical-dependence baseline the pricing signal sits beneath.

title: Energy Technology Perspectives 2026
key_claim: The IEA's flagship Energy Technology Perspectives 2026 puts a special focus on vulnerabilities in energy-technology supply chains and industrial competitiveness, analysing manufacturing capacity, trade flows and materials, and notes governments are working to establish secure and resilient supply chains for clean energy technologies amid high concentration of manufacturing and refining.
frame_summary: The IEA argues that clean-energy-technology and materials supply chains remain dangerously concentrated, making supply-chain resilience a central economic-security question.
notes: Tier 1 IEA flagship; supports the concentration/resilience framing for the physical layer.

title: Critical minerals geopolitics in 2026: risks, supply chains and global power shifts
key_claim: ODI reports that by 2035 China is projected to supply over 60% of refined lithium and cobalt, around 80% of battery-grade graphite and rare earth elements, and approximately 70% of battery-grade manganese; it notes the US is exploring price-support and price-floor mechanisms and direct equity stakes for selected minerals, while the EU's Critical Raw Materials Act has selected 60 Strategic Projects but lacks clear demand and pricing signals such as price floors.
frame_summary: ODI argues China's grip on refining will persist to 2035 and that Western diversification will fail without credible demand and pricing signals, not just projects.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank; refining-dominance projection and the missing-price-signal point central to the thesis.

publisher: Center for Strategic and International Studies
title: Why the West Keeps Losing Critical Mineral Assets to China
key_claim: CSIS reports Chinese firms accelerated overseas mine acquisitions to their highest level in more than a decade in 2024, completing 10 mining transactions worth more than $100 million each, and argues that if China owns the mine it ultimately influences who gets access to the resource, on what terms, and at what price; the US lacks a comprehensive registry of strategic mineral assets and a rapid-response acquisition-financing capability.
frame_summary: CSIS argues China is securing control of future mineral supply at the ownership stage, which lets it shape access, terms and price long before production.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank; the ownership-to-price-control link reinforces that control runs beyond physical output.

title: Volatile, yet robust: Lithium Q1 2026 Price Review
date_evidence: 13th April 2026 3 min read Reported By Adam Megginson
key_claim: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence reports that lithium prices in Q1 2026 were driven by Chinese domestic dynamics: a sharp January rally in Chinese prices on low inventories, government-stimulus expectations and speculative momentum in domestic futures markets, with Benchmark's CIF Asia lithium carbonate spot assessment ending the quarter up about 51% year-to-date despite a more bearish March.
frame_summary: Benchmark shows global lithium price direction in early 2026 was set inside China's domestic and futures markets, not by Western price discovery.
notes: Tier 2 price-reporting agency; evidence that Chinese markets drive global price direction.

title: China to open lithium futures to overseas traders next month (Reuters)
key_claim: China's Guangzhou Futures Exchange will open lithium carbonate futures and options to overseas traders from July 3 2026, with foreign traders able to post US dollars as margin subject to a 5% haircut, in a move Reuters says boosts China's sway over pricing; GFEX dominated global lithium futures with 6.3 million lots of its carbonate contract in May versus 1,051 lots for the CME contract and no trades on the LME's lithium hydroxide contract, following the April internationalisation of nickel futures on the Shanghai Futures Exchange.
frame_summary: Reuters reports China is opening its yuan-denominated lithium futures to foreigners to entrench GFEX as the global pricing benchmark.
notes: Tier 3 (Reuters wire via MINING.COM). The live trigger event for the signal.

title: Column: West needs its own pricing to escape China's rare earths grip (Reuters, Andy Home)
key_claim: Andy Home reports that the reference price for the US Department of Defense's floor-price deal with MP Materials (a $110/kg NdPr floor, with the DoD taking 30% of price upside) is the ex-works China NdPr index compiled by Asian Metal, per MP Materials' regulatory filing, and that under China's 1998 Pricing Law a November 2025 US Select Committee report says it is effectively illegal to publish prices that deviate from the PRC government's wishes; the deal includes an escape clause to switch reference if an internationally recognised ex-China NdPr index is developed; Benchmark Mineral Intelligence has begun collecting ex-China rare-earth prices and the CME and ICE are studying rare-earth futures, while CME lithium volumes grew 37% year-on-year in 2025 with a record 19,590 contracts in January.
frame_summary: Andy Home argues the West cannot escape China's mineral grip with production alone; it must also build its own price-discovery mechanism, and there are early signs it is starting to.
notes: Tier 3 (Reuters columnist via MINING.COM). Load-bearing for the price-control thesis and the Western counter-case.
